title: The Prison We Call Independence
deck: Independence gave us a flag, a date, and a story of freedom. But what happens when the chains are no longer visible—and the prison begins to live inside our minds?
author: Maheen
body: Isn’t the word independence almost cruel in its irony?
We were handed a flag and taught to call it freedom.
We were given a date to celebrate and told that we had been liberated.
But what kind of independence is this, when the people remain prisoners of the very system that claims to protect them?
When a voice raised against injustice becomes an “act of terror,” while the terror inflicted upon the powerless is erased from memory.
When peaceful streets filled with people demanding their rights are reduced to a mob.
When grief is silenced, dissent is criminalized, and obedience is dressed up as patriotism.
Are we independent?
Or have we simply become prisoners who have been taught to decorate the walls of our prison and call it a home?
Perhaps the most terrifying prisons do not have bars.
Perhaps they have flags.
Perhaps they have anthems.
Perhaps they have carefully chosen words like freedom and independence, repeated so often that eventually we stop asking what they mean.
And maybe the illusion extends far beyond governments.
We like to believe that our minds belong to us. That our thoughts are our own. Yet how much of what we believe was planted there before we were even old enough to question it?
We inherit opinions.
We inherit fears.
We inherit prejudices.
We inherit dreams that were never ours.
Then we call ourselves independent thinkers because we chose which trend to follow, which opinion to repeat, which version of ourselves would be most acceptable to the world.
We move with the crowd and call it individuality.
We imitate and call it identity.
We obey and call it choice.
And perhaps that is the darkest kind of captivity—the kind where the prisoner believes the thoughts inside his head are his own.
Sometimes I wonder if I could ever truly free myself from it.
From the hypocrisy.
From the conditioning.
From the desperate need to belong.
From the invisible hands that have shaped the person I think I am.
But even that desire for freedom frightens me.
Because what if the person who wants to escape was created by the very prison they are trying to escape?
What if even our rebellion has been taught to us?

What if change is simply another illusion we cling to because it is easier to believe we can become someone else than to confront the possibility that we may spend our entire lives becoming exactly what the world intended us to be?
Maybe independence was never about breaking chains.
Maybe it is about realizing that the chains exist.
And perhaps the most difficult question is not:
“Are we free?”
But
“If the illusion disappeared tomorrow, would we even recognize freedom when we saw it?
